#1208. Güler scores and assists as Real Madrid win at Mestalla to draw level with Barcelona

Arda Güler scored once and set up another as José Mourinho's Real Madrid beat Valencia 3-0 to reach 30 points, level with Barcelona, before the international break. Valencia are second from bottom in their last season at Mestalla.

Federico Valverde put Madrid ahead at Mestalla in the 28th minute on Saturday 7 November 2026. Güler doubled the lead eight minutes later. Jude Bellingham reached the byline and pulled the ball back. Güler met it first time and finished with his right foot.

Güler could have had more. Stole Dimitrievski stopped him twice: a strong shot from the edge of the area in the 43rd minute and a one-on-one in the 54th.

Kylian Mbappé’s strike in the 75th minute made it three. That goal stretched his scoring run to seven matches in a row. He has 12 league goals, three behind Barcelona’s Raphinha at the top of the scoring chart.

The visitors had 68% of the ball and completed 568 passes to Valencia’s 225. They took 19 shots, 11 of them on target. Valencia managed four shots and just two on target. Expected goals finished 2.39 to 0.26 in Madrid’s favour.

The hosts’ best moment came around the 20th minute. Aaron Mayol won the ball just outside the area and forced Thibaut Courtois to stretch for a save. Aguirre sent on Luis Rioja for Justin de Haas at half-time, but the pattern did not change.

The game grew bad-tempered. Valencia committed 26 fouls to Madrid’s six, and Aguirre himself was booked for dissent in the 59th minute. In the club’s own view, the punishment for Gayà’s challenge on Mbappé was harsh. Seven yellow cards were shown in all, four of them in a two-minute spell after the red card.

Two wins from 12 league games is all Valencia have to show so far. Only Malaga, on 5 points, are below them. Aguirre has one win from his five league games in charge. The club is already promoting season-ticket prices for the new Nou Mestalla.

The coach is concerned about the home form. Aguirre told EFE he was worried about failing to win any of his three matches at Mestalla. He added that Valencia were short of points with six games left in the first half of the season.

#1204. As I sat in the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand, the raw emotion and magic of Old Trafford was all around me. It was a stark reminder that the fans and the place they flock to really are Man United's greatest gift, writes IAN HERBERT

Published: 07:00 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 06:22 EDT, 5 November 2026

The sound came rolling down in waves, crashing down around us as I sat in the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand, in the moments after Manchester United had conceded a most dreadful first goal. It was low and sonorous and quite extraordinary, really.

When a club go nine games without winning and fall behind again, you expect an air of sullen resignation – not that ‘UNITED’ which took hold and grew in a collective, magical act of defiance.

Much more would follow in a significant escalation of protest against the Glazers and their minority partner Sir Jim Ratcliffe. But in that moment – and once more when Roma’s second goal threatened to turn this into a catastrophe – it was just about the terraces and their team. A fanbase refusing to go gently into a night of quiet desperation.

Much has been made of the supposed need to let go of a history which has weighed heavy on this club since Sir Alex stepped away. In turn, United try to release it and then cleave to it again, blindly staggering around in their wilderness.

But on Tuesday night, in the stand bearing the great manager’s name, you looked around and were reminded of how the folk memory of Law, Best, Charlton, Cantona and Rooney is such a powerful weapon. It binds the fans back to what was once great. It is fuel.

What those fans brought into the stadium was not a naive and nostalgic sentimentality. They still demanded the best of the players. There is a clear acceptance among many that Bruno Fernandes is trying to repair things, but when he went down theatrically and protested about a challenge, he was told, ‘stop whinging’.

Michael Carrick celebrates Manchester United's victory over Roma on an incredible Old Trafford Champions League night

Matheus Cunha reacts after scoring United's third goal in their comeback win

This is a discerning, intelligent football public. ‘Standards’ is the word on that banner that’s been flying on the Stretford End.

But the collective view before kick-off was that if the players gave fully, then the fans were with them. ‘I just need to know they’re trying,’ said my friend Jocelyn, as we threaded our way through the crowds to the stadium.

Harry Maguire, who has lived this period of United struggle in the raw and was terribly exposed in a wretched first half, still wore that perpetual look of defiance on his face. When United were fatefully awarded the retaken penalty kick, some were saying that Maguire should be handed the ball. ‘At least he’ll put his foot through it.’

There was a frustration with the way that moments of promise broke down, as passes from Kobbie Mainoo and Carlos Baleba went astray. And with the time it takes Senne Lammens to decide how to distribute the ball, which slows United dreadfully. Yet a recognition of the fight shown by individuals who were patently playing for and engaging with the struggles of Carrick, while contending with a scorching scrutiny.

The shadow on the wall was the owners, of course. It was significant that the chants of derision for them struck up on the Stretford End each time United scored. As if to say that the green and gold campaign won’t fade with the slightest prospect of hope this time. There were tennis balls, balloons and a sense that something is building.

Even now, after 21 years, do the Glazers, hiding in their Florida redoubt, really know that they are playing with fire? This now feels as visceral as Liverpool fans’ hate for Tom Hicks and George Gillett Jnr, 20 years ago.

That club’s fans found ways of getting them out. They email-bombed every outfit that seemed ready to offer to help them, from Royal Bank of Scotland to US equity firm Blackstone. The audible boos when the tennis balls rained down after 20 minutes and five seconds – 20.05 represents the year the Glazers staged their leveraged buy-out – suggests protests affecting play are unwelcome for some and perhaps many. Yet the fury is unbridled. The centre may not hold this time.

The night, however, was about the power of this place to do extraordinary things. Even when Bryan Mbeumo crashed a golden chance to equalise against the post in the early stages of the comeback, you sensed something was afoot.

You’re so close to the pitch in the lower tiers of the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand that you feel you can almost reach out and touch the players. As the stadium gave, so they received. Fernandes marshalled. Youri Tielemans made a difference. Matheus Cunha seized the game by the throat.

Cunha and Shea Lacey race towards the jubilant crowd after United's third goal

And suddenly, like a river, that anthem was taking hold. ‘It’s Carrick you know. It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes’ – over and over again

And suddenly, like a river, that anthem was taking hold. ‘It’s Carrick you know. It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes’ – over and over again. At the end Diego Dalot was flat out on his back before us. Mason Mount, who’d been on the field barely five minutes, was in delirium and the post-match acknowledgement of fans by Carrick with his players felt like a victory lap. It meant that much.

The Carrick anthem was still being sung on the concourses as we flooded out under the clear night sky, and you knew for sure in that moment why no one wants the distinctly average names like Eddie Howe, Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann being touted for this job.

‘I don’t want us to start all over again,’ Jocelyn told me, still trying to compute what we’d just seen, after we'd joined the departing throng. ‘I want Carrick to do it. I want more nights like this.’

We learned in the aftermath that Carrick’s career-saving half-time speech had involved him telling his players how Old Trafford could do this. ‘I don't like to keep talking to the lads about what this place can do and the history and what's gone before too much, but it's there,’ he said. ‘This place does magical things. It's done it before and it'll do it over and over again.’

Yes, that really did encapsulate the essence of a night on which we discovered, once more, that the fans and the place they flock to really are Manchester United's greatest gift.

#1201. Clearing the way for a transformative stem-cell treatment for Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Joohi Jimenez-Shahed studies movement disorders, neuromodulation and brain circuit therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Big improvements in Parkinson’s disease treatment have been few and far between. The tantalizing prospect of regenerative stem-cell therapies to address this neurodegenerative condition is therefore creating considerable excitement.

A core component of Parkinson’s is the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, which normally provide carefully controlled neurotransmitter signals to the brain’s movement circuits1. This leads to people having substantial difficulties performing routine activities.

A dopamine-replacement approach provided one of the first major advances in Parkinson’s treatment2. Levodopa, a chemical precursor to dopamine that was introduced in the 1960s, treats symptoms effectively. But the levodopa honeymoon can be short. As the effect duration of each dose wanes, extra doses or medications are required to keep dopamine levels from falling. And the drug can come with a complication that many patients dread — writhing, uncontrolled involuntary movements known as dyskinesia. A surgical approach called deep brain stimulation (DBS) can mitigate these complications effectively3.

The downsides of levodopa raise a question: rather than replacing dopamine, why not replace the cellular machinery that produces it? Enter the dopaminergic stem cell. Engineered from cells sampled from an adult’s own tissues (known as autologous) or from a different individual (allogeneic), induced-pluripotent stem cells can be safely transplanted into human brains and can improve movement-related Parkinson’s symptoms, such as tremors, stiffness and slowness, without worsening dyskinesia4.

Only a few dozen people have received this experimental treatment. Major brain surgery is required to transplant the cells. Allogeneic cell transplants also require recipients to undertake a year of immunosuppression to ensure that the cells survive. Autologous cell transplants avoid this, but it takes 6–8 months to produce the cells for each patient.

It is not yet known how cell therapies will measure up to current standards of care. Early studies have been in people with advanced disease. At this stage, the chance of benefit might be reduced: the cells are implanted into an already degenerating circuit that could be difficult to restore.

Critics might therefore argue that dopamine cell therapies cannot produce a more robust effect than levodopa or DBS without imposing excess cost or risk. But the way that Parkinson’s treatments are investigated and approved can neither fully support this pessimistic view nor provide sufficient evidence for a more optimistic one.

Therapeutic development for Parkinson’s has mainly aimed to relieve symptoms. A more ambitious goal would be to slow the disease’s progression by altering its underlying biology. Yet there are substantial obstacles to developing such a treatment.

Implicit to the concept of disease modification is the need for a biomarker that measures the underlying biological processes5. Although a biological definition of Parkinson’s is emerging, it applies mainly to the identification of early disease. Relatively little is known about how such markers evolve in Parkinson’s, or how they relate to clinical progression6.

Long-term, multi-site observational studies such as the Parkinson’s Precision Medicine Initiative (see go.nature.com/4ayapbI) provide an ideal framework for exploring digital, biological and imaging markers, while benchmarking disease progression. Their success depends on building and sustaining large consortia, and on a healthy dose of time and effort from researchers and study participants, but the studies are constrained by funding inequities.

Even if such biomarkers were already at researchers’ disposal, there is no specific guidance from the US Food and Drug Administration on developing disease-modifying treatments7. The agency’s Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy designation speeds up cell- and gene-therapy development and approval. But eligibility requires only the intent to treat, modify, reverse or cure a serious disorder. As a result, clinical trials of regenerative therapies are likely to be designed to show benefits to a person’s symptoms without incurring the added cost and burden of showing a change in biology — a pragmatic but less ambitious path.

Crucially, supportive evidence for the broader potential of dopaminergic cell therapies is what will define their advantage. Cell dose, optimal treatment timing and objective evidence of cell survival, engraftment and effects on brain-network function would demonstrate whether cell therapies can produce lasting change in people with Parkinson’s. Public–private research partnerships could refine the required measurement tools and generate such data.

The ability to transform stem cells into dopamine-producing neurons and transplant them safely into human brains is momentous. Its use as a treatment extends an opportunity to chart another course for people with Parkinson’s by limiting levodopa complications and possibly the need for DBS. This outcome would bolster the hopes of people with this condition. But the real therapeutic breakthrough will occur only when scientists and regulators converge to advance the goal of restoring neural circuitry and function. That would be a truly bold step towards conquering this this relentless disease.

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of important saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

“I prefer to speak about the saves that he made,” the Villa manager said. “This is part of football. I think he played fantastically and he is doing a lot of saves so he can make one mistake. It is part of football. We can be mature about this.

“I still want to see consistency. Over the last five Premier League matches, we are winning three and drawing two. It’s not bad but with our poor start it’s not enough.

“We have to change our mind quickly for Tuesday against Barcelona. We want to test ourselves at this level.”

Villa go to the Nou Camp with a 100 per cent Champions League record to their name this season. But they will need to improve on Saturday evening’s performance to get a result in Spain.

As well as Suzuki’s error, a 14th-minute penalty miss from John McGinn also proved costly.

It was awarded after Leon Goretzka, making his full league debut for Villa, saw his header hit Sander Berge’s raised hand. Nobody appealed at the time but referee Sam Barrott was sent to the touchline monitor by VAR to review the incident and gave the spot-kick.

McGinn’s attempt, however, hit the crossbar and the chance to take an early lead went begging. The Villa captain seemed a strange choice to take the spot-kick as he has only ever scored one career penalty, but Emery defended the choice, saying: “We analysed the penalty takers in the squad and it was McGinn here.”

Nicolas Jackson was on hand to ease Villa’s nerves before the break, though. the Villa manager had said before the game that the striker’s goalscoring capability meant he was capable of matching the likes of Harry Kane. Collecting Johan Manzambi’s superbly weighted pass, Jackson forced his way past two defenders before sliding in the goal that put Villa ahead.

Zion Suzuki had big gloves to fill this summer after the sale of Emiliano Martínez but already appears one of the Premier League signings of the summer.

Aston Villa’s new No 1 epitomises the vibrant energy of Unai Emery’s revamped squad and is a goalkeeper perfectly suited to the modern game.

The Japanese international is Villa’s own version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson, who revolutionised English football with a vast range of passing from his own penalty area.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

Sawiris’s short statement, which he published on social media on Friday night, consisted of 37 ill-chosen words. It started by accusing Carragher of “unacceptable insults to the club and its fans”, then concluded with the vainglorious declaration that “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football”.

Aston Villa manager, Unai Emery, is giving a full Premier League debut to Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka against Fulham this evening.

The 31-year-old joined Villa on a free transfer in the summer, but a knee injury prevented him from making an appearance off the bench until this month’s Champions League tie against Fenerbahce.

Asked what role Goretzka would have with Villa, Emery deadpanned: “The first one is to be available to play.”

Emery had also made a cryptic remark about Nicolas Jackson and Johann Manzambi in his Friday press conference. The suggestion was that they had been merely rested for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup defeat at Bournemouth.

But the Spaniard said: “For different reasons, not only rest.”

Whatever he meant is unclear, but both start for Villa tonight.

Fulham have won their last two league games – against Hull and Coventry.

Manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, has made one change with Sander Berge replacing Hugo Larsson in midfield.

Villa are aiming to win three successive league games for the first time in this calendar year. The omens are good as they’ve beaten Fulham in their last seven league meetings at Villa Park.

Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

#1195. Premier League star's career criminal brother beats Home Office bid to deport him to Africa - as he awaits trial for kidnap, false imprisonment, aggravated burglary and robbery

Published: 03:45 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 04:38 EDT, 8 November 2026

The street criminal brother of a Premier League star has beaten a Home Office attempt to deport him to Africa - by citing his own human rights.

The gang member and aspiring rapper, now in his twenties, was the subject of a concerted four year attempt by the government to send him to his family's country of origin in West Africa because of his shocking criminal record.

The young man, who has never held down a job, is currently in prison for dangerous driving and carrying a knife - while awaiting yet another court case accused of kidnap, false imprisonment, aggravated burglary and robbery.

During his teens he had played academy football for several Premier League teams but while his brother went on to make it and is now a multi-millionaire, the man instead got sucked into street crime.

And he has been involved in so much anti-social and criminal behaviour since then that he has even incurred a number of gunshot wounds.

But the wannabe rapper has managed to win a long-running deportation bid by the Home Office to kick him out of Britain as an undesirable - arguing that this wouldn't be fair as all his significant ties are here.

A Premier League footballer - who cannot be named for legal reasons - has seen his career criminal brother living in Britian beat a Home Office attempt to deport him back to West Africa

The Home Office first targeted him for deportation in 2022 after he was sentenced to 20 months in jail having been caught with a sword in his waistband, which in turn meant had breached an existing order about his criminal behaviour.

They lost that attempt to get him out of Britain but appealed - and have now lost that appeal too.

The gang member is 'healthy and capable' according to a judge but has never worked - in stark contrast to his hugely successful brother, a full international footballer who has made countless top flight appearances.

A court heard the foreign national has a 'sustained history of criminal offending involving repeated breaches of Criminal Behaviour Orders, possession of offensive weapons, breaches of licence conditions, recalls to custody, and recent charges. He has a history of offending with knives since the age of 17'.

Totaling his various jail terms together he has spent three of the last eight years prison.

But despite his ongoing recurrent criminality, the Home Office has failed in its latest attempt to deport him after a judge ruled he is 'socially and culturally integrated' into the UK and a return to his home country would leave him 'very much an outsider'.

The immigration tribunal decided he would face 'very significant obstacles to integration' in his home country and prevented the government from deporting him by ruling it would breach his human rights.

That decision came despite it emerging that he has an uncle in the country and grew up with a familiarity of the country, including its culture and food, while his mother maintains links to the country and visited as recently as 2024.

But the judge said the 'significance of these ties should not be exaggerated' because he has never been there.

They said his social and cultural identity 'has been almost entirely formed in the UK and by British culture' - even though he was born overseas and his family come from West Africa. The Home Office is appealing the decision and so the brother could still face deporation.

The knife criminal first arrived in the UK in 2006 after being born in another country where he doesn't have nationality.

He is in a relationship with a British woman with whom he shares a baby.

Their child was born in February but the rapper has only met them twice because he remains incarcerated.

There is no evidence that having a partner or child has reformed his criminal ways, a court heard.

The Home Office argued he is a healthy young adult capable of work who has a familiarity with the culture of his home country and has family ties in the country who could provide guidance and support.

But the judge concluded it would breach his human rights because he has never lived or visited and would be an outsider if returned.

An outbreak of anthrax has killed at least 30 hippos (Hippopotamus amphibius) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in the past month. No cases of the infectious disease have been reported in people so far. The wildlife outbreak puts further pressure on already limited resources, say researchers, as the DRC grapples with armed conflict and large outbreaks of Ebola and cholera.

Contributions to a United Nations-run pot for the conservation of nature — expected to raise US$1 billion per year — total just US$10,588 two years after it was established. The Cali Fund seeks voluntary contributions from companies that profit from genetic data collected from Earth’s biodiversity. So far, only five small biotech companies have contributed.

In the 2026 fiscal year, which ended on 30 September, the US National Science Foundation (NSF) funded fewer than 100 new social-science grants, compared with a historical average of roughly 850 per year. In dozens of programme areas, including economics and archaeology, the agency awarded no new grants at all. Earlier this year, the administration of President Donald Trump stated that it wants to eliminate the NSF’s social, behavioural and economic sciences (SBE) directorate altogether, leaving several decades-long projects hanging in the balance.

A study in mice might help explain the long-known fact that castration extends life span in most mammals, including people — and why men tend to live shorter lives than women. In the experiment, researchers removed the testicles of mice before puberty, after puberty or in old age, and found that all interventions increased median lifespan — with the late intervention leading to the biggest improvement. The findings suggest that testes’ apparently harmful effects begin later in life, rather than during their puberty heyday.

Widespread migration of people from countryside to cities is leading to a surprising drop in biodiversity in some of the low-intensity farming landscapes where humans have lived in harmony with other creatures for millennia. For example, in Japan, forests where farmers once cut trees for fuel and removed fallen leaves for fertilizer are becoming dense and closed in again — leading to losses in species such as fireflies and harvest mice. Volunteers have taken up saws to help, but experts say that longer-term solutions are needed, such as rewilding or addressing rural depopulation.

When Edward Freytag, a 66-year-old music teacher, injured his brain in a motorcycle crash, he developed the ability to instantly recognize musical notes. He’s the first person known to have acquired perfect pitch from a brain injury. In this beautifully illustrated feature, explore how our brains process sound, learn how Freytag’s injury might have affected him this way, and listen to a composition he wrote in a fugue-like state during the early stages of his recovery.

#1186. Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

“There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

The result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

It might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola said Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

“That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

“That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta said. And that was indisputable.

Even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

In fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

There was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

#1179. From last place to the playoffs: How the Philadelphia Union pulled off MLS's most stunning turnaround

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

CHESTER, Pa. -- At the end of the World Cup, the Philadelphia Union were at the bottom of the Eastern Conference and all of Major League Soccer with only seven points, moving on from Supporters' Shield-winning head coach Bradley Carnell and turning to 36-year-old Ryan Richter to save the season. Given Richter's path as someone who oversaw the Union's MLS Next Pro side before becoming an assistant under Jim Curtin with the first team, it seemed like a moment where the Union would be in the process of preparing for next season and seeing what they did next.

But with the return of a familiar face in Kai Wagner, a meeting at Two Persons Coffee in South Philadelphia between captain Alejandro Bedoya and Richter, and one of the most impressive runs that we've seen of youth talent in league history, the Union were able to clinch a place in the MLS Cup playoffs, and they did it in impressive fashion, too, by playing Nashville SC to a scoreless draw away from home without 17-year-old phenom Cavan Sullivan being available for the match. It caps off a turnaround that has seen the Union pick up 40 points since the World Cup, winning 12 matches, drawing four, and only losing one. Those 40 points outpace the second-best team in the time range, which is Nashville SC, by five.

Sullivan has been one of the spark plugs of this improvement with seven goals and 11 assists, with most of that coming after the World Cup break, but with 38 of the Union's 59 league goals absent for that game as Bruno Damiani and Milan Iloski missed out on the match, it truly showed the mentality that the squad has.

Plenty preach about "next-man-up" mentality, but matches like this one show why no one should want to face the Union in the playoffs. If the season ended today, they'd face Inter Miami in a three-game series, which would be sure to bring fireworks after the scuffle that their last meeting created, but there's still more work to do with two games remaining, as the Union could slide down to the eight-versus-nine play-in game if they lose their final two games of the regular season.

Under Carnell, the Union were a traditional high-press team that tried to force their opponents into mistakes. While it worked with only MLS games to play, adding in the Concacaf Champions Cup saw the team unable to keep up that intensity, especially without Wagner at left back and with Neil Pierre on loan in Denmark instead of being with the squad. While Richter did benefit from both of these players being in the mix, he has also dialed things back to more of a zonal press, allowing the midfield to have time to rest in between plays so that they can keep the same intensity at minute 90 as they have entering the game.

Pierre and Nathan Harriel on the back line have assisted greatly with that, being mobile centerbacks in their own right. Richter knows the impact of having a 6-foot-7 defender like Pierre, who is also comfortable when being on an island, and it's clear how he helps the attack function.

"We can be super aggressive because Neil is comfortable in one-on-one situations. If it's a direct ball, he wins; he eats all of these. If it's open space that he has to defend, physically, he can deal with that, and he's also a good defender," Richter said. "The way he puts out so many fires allows us to be aggressive higher up the field, because we know when they play the ball long that we have someone who cleans this up almost every time."

Putting that in front of three-time MLS Goalkeeper of the Year Andre Blake, it's easy to see why the Union's defense has improved from the first half of the season, but the attack is where major strides have been made.

You'd have to be living under a rock to have not heard the name Cavan Sullivan by now, and for good reason, as the 17-year-old has been taking MLS by storm and helping push the Union attack forward with his creativity. Since the World Cup break, Sullivan is second only to Evander in assists with nine and has pitched in goals alongside that. He may not be the biggest or fastest player on the pitch, but the quick bursts that he has into space have been tormenting defenses.

Alongside Pierre and Frankie Westfield, he was able to earn his first national team cap under Mauricio Pochettino and also didn't look out of place there either, but when speaking to him and people around the team, the shift in mentality is clear. Sullivan asked to do extra training during the World Cup break instead of taking the time off, and has come back a more complete player. Already set to join Manchester City when he turns 18 next year, the path for future development is clear (assuming City are in the Premier League), but this is one of the best American soccer prospects ever developed. Being able to play alongside his older brother Quinn also helps with this transition, but Cavan has grown into a player of his own, and while this season has been a coming-out party for him in many ways, the playoffs are going to be a moment that can thrust him into the stratosphere as he looks to lead his hometown club to the first MLS Cup title in their history.

Which American has the most goals in Major League Soccer? Usually, the answer to that question is Brian White, but this season, it also resides in Philadelphia in Milan Iloski, a longtime journeyman, he has found a home in Philadelphia and has scored 19 goals with seven assists, which is third in the league. After moving Tai Baribo to D.C. United, there were valid questions of where the Union's goals would come from, and Iloski has delivered and shown that there isn't a finish that he doesn't have in his locker, and he's not overperforming, either, with an xG of 18.77.

Alongside him, Bruno Damiani has stepped up with 12 goals, and the Uruguayan could be key to any serious playoff run that the team has. If teams crowd Sullivan and Iloski, other people on the team need to be able to make them pay, and Damiani is chief among them. The hope was that new signing Ezekiel Alladoh would be able to take on that mantle, but with one goal and one assist in 26 appearances, he may find minutes hard to come by in the playoffs unless there's an injury. While it's unlikely that they'd upset the likes of Nashville and Miami to win the MLS Cup, the mantra of "Why not us" has always carried Philadelphia and looking at these numbers, you can't say that they don't have a chance. Given that, it is also only a matter of time until the interim tag is removed from Richter's coaching title, but that's an offseason issue to deal with; right now, there are more soccer games to win.

The players listed are in no specific order; they're just driving the conversation around the game in their own way.

If you're following along, you can check out our previous Star Power Index.

Among a handful of U.S. women's national team players currently injured or benched with clubs active in the Champions League, there is a player who shines just a bit brighter at the moment. OL Lyonnes midfielder Lily Yohannes is back in the Star Power Index after a stellar performance against Inter Milan. She was part of a midfield trio alongside Melchie Dumornay and Damaris Egurrola that dominated the middle third of the pitch against the tournament debutants.

Shortly before the hour mark, Dumornay's attempt on goal had just been ruled out after a foul on the play, and the heads-up quick play by the 19-year-old Yohannes resulting in scoring a crazy long-distance lob that chipped the goalkeeper. It's her second chipped goal in the tournament, and it just adds to OL's stacked attack.

Most of the attacking play ran through Kaptein who was able to pick out runners in the buildup and find space between Roma's lines with deep passes.

She set up both assists on goals Ellie Carpenter and Kadeisha Buchanan, following up her lone goal game-winner performance against Austria Wien on opening day. The win now gives Chelsea seven points and puts them among the top four of the league phase table.

The Italian international scored in the 38th minute and again just six minutes later, despite more chances created by OH Leuven. Servette's attack was far more ruthless, all capped by Marinelli's quick brace. It's the first win for the Swiss side, and a crucial three points at the halfway mark of the competition.

#1176. Forest Green apologise for failing to commemorate Remembrance Day at a home match due to 'mistake'

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 10:15 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 10:43 EDT, 8 November 2026

Forest Green Rovers have apologised for failing to commemorate Remembrance Day at a home game, labelling it as 'human error' and a 'mistake' from the club.

Remembrance Day is November 11 with Forest Green's sole fixture around that date having been Saturday's 2-0 FA Cup first-round defeat at Luton Town. Both teams commemorated the occasion ahead of kick-off at Kenilworth Road.

Forest Green's last home fixture prior to that was a 2-2 draw with Harrogate Town on October 31 in the National League.

That encounter at The New Lawn saw supporters of the fifth-tier side take to a fan forum post-match questioning why nothing was in place for Remembrance Day - due to their then-forthcoming clash with Luton being an away tie.

Forest Green owner Dale Vince replied on the club's Fan Advisory Board, admitting it was an oversight on their part.

'The lack of Remembrance at a home game is simply down to a human error/mistake on the club,' he wrote.

Forest Green Rovers have apologised for not commemorating Remembrance Day at a home game (National League side pictured doing so during Saturday's FA Cup 2-0 defeat at Luton)

Forest Green failed to do so in their home draw vs Harrogate on October 31, calling it a 'mistake'

Forest Green Rovers owner Dale Vince has vowed that to contact the Royal British Legion for advice on future commemorations to ensure this wouldn't happen again

Vince continued that a condensed schedule in this period didn't help matters, but still acknowledged that the club should have done more.

'It didn't help that we had a sizable number of games in a small time frame (including the FA Cup replay) beforehand; albeit that isn't an excuse, we should have got this right.'

Following the incident, the 65-year-old confirmed that Forest Green would contact the Royal British Legion for advice on future commemorations to ensure this wouldn't happen again. He also underlined that the missed home commemoration did not signal any change in the club's support for Remembrance or the Royal British Legion.

'This was a simple error/mistake,' he reiterated.

#1174. Inter and AC Milan unveil plans for new 71,500-seat Generali Stadium to replace iconic San Siro

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It was an historic day in Milan as Inter and AC Milan have finally unveiled the project for the new stadium that will replace San Siro, the current arena that hosts the home games of both teams. The new San Siro will be named "Generali Stadium" after the Italian insurance company Generali acquired the naming rights of the stadium in a deal worth €650 million ($725 million) over 20 years, according to multiple reports. The Generali Stadium will be ready by the 2031-2032 season, according to the two clubs, just in time for the UEFA 2032 Euro that will be co-hosted by Italy and Turkiye, with construction starting in 2028. The current San Siro will be demolished only after the new stadium is ready to be used by the teams, giving more time for fans to attend a match in the iconic Italian stadium that was built in 1926.

Let's now go into the details of the new arena: According to the joint news release from both clubs, it will be a "71,500-seat stadium designed around one of football's most iconic atmospheres, setting a new standard for the live fan experience". A bold architectural vision by Foster + Partners and MANICA, bringing together Lord Norman Foster and David Manica, the two architects who previously worked on the design of London's Wembley Stadium. The new arena will feature a striking X-frame structure and a sweeping double-curved roof, conceived to become Milan's next landmark. A "defining investment" by RedBird and Oaktree, AC Milan and Inter ownerships, to "strengthen sporting competitiveness, unlock future growth and help shape the next era of Italian football".

Two seating tiers form a continuous 360-degree bowl, creating exceptional sightlines and an immersive connection between fans and pitch. At either end, the iconic Curvas rise as single, steep walls of support, drawn forward toward the field of play with seating inclinations of up to 37 degrees to amplify both atmosphere and visual impact. At the heart of the design is a striking structural form, whose powerful rhythm recalls both the legacy of Italian engineering and the intricate craftsmanship of the Duomo di Milano.

Engineered to capture and intensify crowd energy, the stadium's acoustic design ensures supporters remain at the heart of the spectacle, helping create an environment designed to be among the most atmospheric in world football. Enhanced accessibility, modern hospitality concepts and a broad range of seating options, from world-class premium experiences to popular seating areas, will ensure the venue welcomes every generation of fan, while offering new ways to experience the game.

The two teams will continue to share their home stadium, a unique tradition that started in the late '40's of the 20th century, when Inter moved to San Siro as well. Unlike most of the teams around the world of soccer, Inter and AC Milan decided to continue sharing their home stadium after leaving the current arena. After years of failed projects and attempts, the new stadium is now a concrete reality. In 2025, the Milan City Council approved the sale of the city's San Siro stadium to the two clubs Inter and AC Milan. Now, the two Italian teams have decided to move into a new direction and era.

As Italian soccer is facing a crisis also regarding their infrastructures, the Generali Stadium can drastically increase the match revenues of both Inter and AC Milan, putting them at the level of the European rivals. At the same time, seeing the teams leave the legendary San Siro will be hard.

San Siro has been the home of AC Milan and Inter, but its history extends far beyond soccer. The iconic stadium has hosted some of the most memorable sporting and cultural events, including the opening ceremony of the 2026 Winter Olympic Games and legendary concerts by some of the biggest names in music. From Bob Marley's historic performance in 1980, the first-ever concert at San Siro, to unforgettable shows by the Rolling Stones, David Bowie, Michael Jackson, Madonna, Taylor Swift, U2 or Bruce Springsteen, who has famously described San Siro as his second home, the stadium has become a landmark far beyond the world of sport. Now, a new era is about to start but the "old" San Siro won't be forgotten.

Un nuovo simbolo per Milano.Una nuova casa per le future generazioni di tifosi Interisti.​Generali Stadium 🏟️ ‌ pic.twitter.com/9wmNGfrVI9

#1173. How the brain protects itself from Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Sarah DeWeerdt is a science journalist in Seattle, Washington.

The pianist’s hands are poised over the keys, his right hand trembles slightly. A drummer and bass player start up and, after a beat, the pianist joins in, both hands fluently producing the luscious, staccato rhythms of jazz.

The hands in this video from 2019 belong to Dutch musician René van Helsdingen, who had recently been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. He uses strategies that reduce stress and emotion to help quiet the tremors that affect his right side and enable him to continue playing the music he loves, he explains in the video. “It’s my improvised solution.”

Improvisation is an apt metaphor for the ways in which many people with Parkinson’s learn to cope with the tremor, stiffness and movement difficulties that are characteristic of the neurodegenerative disease. Some use an external source of rhythm, such as a metronome, to overcome the tendency to ‘freeze up’ when walking or adopt a sideways crab-like gait. “I’m very inspired” by people’s creativity, says Rick Helmich, a neurologist at Radboud University in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, who has worked with van Helsdingen.

Other improvisations take place in the brain, beyond a person’s awareness, to preserve function in the face of Parkinson’s pathology. If scientists can understand them better and harness them more effectively, they might be able to slow the progression of Parkinson’s disease, delay its onset and even prevent it entirely, say researchers, such as Helmich.

The motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease are caused by a loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra — part of a set of structures nestled deep in the brain known as the basal ganglia. But these symptoms do not emerge until at least 30% of those neurons are lost, and sometimes as many as 70%. Two people with a similar degree of neurodegeneration might have very different symptom severity. And some people’s condition worsens quickly, whereas others remain stable for years. Such observations have led most researchers and clinicians to agree that brain-based mechanisms of resilience must be important.

But for a long time, this area received little research attention because scientists focused instead on unravelling the pathology of the disease and on developing an effective treatment, called levodopa, that remedied the underlying dopamine loss. The awareness that the brain has ways of making up for the neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s hasn’t led to clinical advances, says Thilo van Eimeren, a specialist in brain imaging at the University of Cologne in Germany.

This area is now garnering more interest. It is a focus of a three-year, European Union-funded project launched in 2025, known as TRACE-PD, to track the mechanisms of disease progression and functional compensation in early stages of disease1.

The first task for the team from across Europe was to define its terms. That effort is more than mere semantics, says David Pedrosa, a neurologist at Marburg University in Germany and co-coordinator of the project. More clarity in the vocabulary that researchers use to talk about protective mechanisms will enable them to probe the underlying biology with greater precision, and design better targeted clinical trials to investigate how to bolster these processes, he explains.

The TRACE-PD consortium has defined resilience as an umbrella term that encompasses multiple protective mechanisms. One, called reserve, refers to neuronal resources built up across the lifespan that mitigate the effects of the disease. Another, called compensation, involves changes to neurons and brain networks that stabilize function in response to the disease.

The idea behind reserve makes intuitive sense: when a neurodegenerative process takes hold, individuals who have greater neural resources in a particular domain will take longer to decline to a point at which their impairment becomes obvious. Cognitive reserve has long been a focus of Alzheimer’s disease research. And over the past few years, studies of Parkinson’s have examined the idea of motor reserve.

Most such studies have defined individuals with high motor reserve as those with milder motor symptoms than their degree of dopamine-neuron loss would predict. A 2020 study by researchers in South Korea showed that people with newly diagnosed Parkinson’s and high motor reserve have greater connectivity between areas of the brain involved in movement, planning and control2. Greater connectivity in this network is also linked to a lower need for levodopa treatment.

“Individuals with higher motor reserve levels also show greater grey matter volume in motor-associated areas,” says Merle Hönig, a neuropsychologist at the University of Cologne. She and van Eimeren contributed to a study3 that also found that the gap in disease trajectory between individuals with high motor reserve and low motor reserve takes more than seven years to close, suggesting that assessing motor reserve early could help to determine prognosis.

But could motor reserve be the basis for interventions to alter the course of Parkinson’s? The same study showed an association between higher motor reserve and higher levels of physical activity in one cohort of people with the disease — a suggestive but circumstantial link. The team now has unpublished data that strengthen the case for a causal relationship by showing that people with higher lifetime levels of physical activity also have higher motor reserve. Exercise is known to slow progression during the early phases of Parkinson’s, but there is much about this connection that is poorly understood, says Patrick Santens, a neurologist at Ghent University in Belgium. “Nobody really knows what is the best,” he says. What type of exercise is beneficial, at what intensity and for which individuals?

Another question is the relationship between the different types of reserve. “We don’t know whether promoting, for example, cognitive reserve also helps to preserve motor reserve,” or vice versa, Hönig says. Research in this area might, therefore, have implications for multiple neurodegenerative diseases.

Research involving compensation goes back to at least the early 1990s. But over the past few years, Helmich says, the concept has been refined. Whereas greater activity in a brain area or network was once seen as evidence of compensation, scientists are now looking for a link between stronger hyperactivity and greater symptom reduction, for example.

This approach has enabled researchers to zero in on the neural substrate of compensation. Helmich and his team have shown that the main brain areas involved are the parietal cortex and the premotor cortex. The less affected parts of the basal ganglia also contribute4.

Another group have investigated brain activity in people with dopamine-neuron loss on both sides of the brain, but symptoms on only one side of the body. The researchers identified several compensatory mechanisms in the brain hemisphere that controls the unaffected side of the body, including increased plasticity in motor networks5.

Helmich and his team have also shown6 that, over the course of two years, “the speed of progression relates to the collapse of compensatory mechanisms”, he says. The researchers have unpublished data from a separate cohort showing that people who have mutations in the gene encoding the enzyme glucocerebrosidase, long known to increase the risk of Parkinson’s, have reduced potential for compensation. Such studies place the loss of compensation at the centre of disease progression.

Researchers are now beginning to investigate how to intervene to stimulate compensatory mechanisms. Helmich and his team identified an ‘anti tremor network’ that comes online when a tremor reduces in intensity and consists of areas of the cortex involved in attention and in interpreting bodily sensations7. He is testing whether an intervention involving mindfulness training and meditation can help people to activate this network and control the tremor.

Stimulating compensatory mechanisms might also involve non-invasive brain stimulation — Helmich plans to launch a study later this year using transcranial ultrasound to activate the less affected parts of the basal ganglia to find out. Meanwhile, Pedrosa is investigating how to use advancing knowledge of compensation to improve deep-brain stimulation, a treatment in which electrodes are implanted in the brain to send electrical signals to areas involved in motor control.

Further research will be needed to help refine and guide these approaches, says Josefine Waldthaler, a neuroimaging specialist at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden. “We know where to look” for compensation in the cerebral cortex, Waldthaler says, but not the particular patterns of brain activity that define it, and therefore what brain frequency interventions need to stimulate.

Magnetoencephalography, an imaging method that is Waldthaler’s specialty, could fill in some of those details. And that’s where TRACE-PD comes in. The effort brings together researchers who use different approaches to investigate various aspects of resilience. Rather than collect new data, the idea is to share existing data sets and analytical methods. This will help the consortium to tease apart the mechanisms of compensation and reserve, validate definitions and refine applications, Pedrosa says. What the researchers find could have broader relevance as well. “The cool thing about the idea of compensation and reserve is that it’s not a Parkinson’s specific idea,” says Pedrosa. He contends that the group’s insights might shed light on other neurodegenerative conditions, such as Alzheimer’s disease, as well as on strategies for healthy ageing.

And although TRACE-PD focuses on early Parkinson’s, the processes it looks at might still be harnessed later in the disease. In May, van Helsdingen performed with his trio in Italy. In a video of the concert, his symptoms seem to have worsened since 2019. He rocks rhythmically back and forth as he plays, and at one point crosses his left wrist over his right to execute a particularly tricky sequence of notes on the upper keys with his less-affected left hand. But the result is syncopated, at times cheerful, music that makes it clear he’s still improvising.

#1170. To infinity and beyond! Another stunning Diego Gomez strike has Brighton up to SECOND and daring to dream... as Brentford's Igor Thiago is goaded into a red card

Published: 11:08 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 12:40 EDT, 8 November 2026

Onwards and upwards go Brighton. Another victory to send them soaring into second place with only Arsenal above them.

It is a lofty perch for the Seagulls and one more admirable when considering the depths from which they have risen.

Homeless and penniless, on the brink of extinction at the end of the last century they are now daring to dream about the Champions League.

To infinity and beyond. Why not? Fabian Hurzeler’s team have already beaten Arsenal and Manchester City without conceding this season.

The only goals scored against them in the last six Premier League games came at Liverpool, where they lost 2-0 but were not outplayed.

City’s season is mired in uncertainty, awaiting sentence for financial breaches and the other half of the traditional Big Six are so erratic there will likely be scope for interlopers when the prized European tickets are handed out in May.

It is six months away but at this moment in time there are not four teams better than Fabian Hurzeler’s.

Brighton appear fully formed. Delightfully fluent in attack. Creative with zip and imagination and different ways to score goals.

There is a defined style of play. Solid at the back with enough sporting maturity to survive a test of needle, which this became against Brentford after the red card for Igor Thiago’s red card.

Diego Gomez celebrated another memorable strike at the Amex Stadium after his halfway-line stunner in the 5-0 win over Crystal Palace

The Bees already trailed to a screamer from the left boot of Diego Gomez and went further behind before half time when Pascal Gross converted a penalty awarded for a shirt pull by Keane Lewis-Potter on Luka Vuskovic.

Brighton (4-2-3-1): Verbruggen 6; Costinha 6, Dunk 6, Vuskovic 6, Boscagli 7; Gross 8, Andres 6 (Wieffer 46, ); Gomez 7 (Yalcoue 90+3), Ayari 7 (Hinshelwood 78), De Cuyper 7 (Minteh 82); Kostoulas 6 (Rutter 82)

Subs not used: Steele, Hadjam, Kadioglu, Svoboda

Bookings: Andres, Boscagli, Wieffer, Dunk

Brentford (4-3-3): Kelleher 6; Kayode 5, Ajer 6, Van den Berg 6 (Wilson 70), Lewis-Potter 5 (Diouf 59); Sangare 5 (Jensen 59), Janelt 5, Hickey 5 (Collins 46); Ouattara 4 (Yarmoliuk 46), Thiago 3, Schade 4

Subs not used: Valdimarsson, Anthony, Damsgaard, Schuster

Gross, the 35-year-old midfielder schemer who walloped his penalty into the top corner in emphatic fashion, embodies the confidence pulsing through this team and his goal closed the contest.

The Bees assembled in the deep looking to minimise damage with an eye on a counterattack or a set piece and maybe hoping the officials would see fit to even it up at 10 against 10.

It didn’t happen. Instead, Brighton controlled the ball. They have had more than 75 per cent of possession across 90 minutes and spent the second half probing around the fringes of the Brentford penalty area.

They registered 20 shots in all but there would be no third goal. And nobody minded. They celebrated the victory and a return to the Amex Stadium after five away games in a row and more than 5,000 miles on the road.

Every substitution made by Hurzeler came as a reminder of their strength and quality.

Kaoru Mitoma, yet to feature this season, is expected back from injury soon after the international break.

The Conference League is not proving a distraction to a squad of such depth and Hurzeler gave fans his permission to dream.

'They should be always excited,' said the Brighton boss. 'That’s our job. They can dream. They can have high expectations, but these are things we can’t control. We played good game but always things we can do better.'

This was Brentford’s second defeat in this Premier League season and they had players sent off in both.

'In both scenarios the opposition player has been the one to provoke the situation, antagonise our player and react towards our player in an aggressive way,' fumed boss Keith Andrews, referring to Yehor Yarmoliuk’s red card against Liverpool, when the Bees finished the game with nine men.

'We should do better, but the game is in a state now and a place I don’t particularly like. And we’ll have to have a look at that because it’s costing us.'

Chema Andres fouled Thiago, fell to the ground and sprang up to confront the Brazilian, who tried to push him away but caught him with a forearm under the jaw.

Igor Thiago's yellow card was upgraded to red after a VAR intervention

Andres collapsed for a second time. When Michael Oliver gave them a yellow card each it seemed fair, but VAR Stuart Attwell sent the referee to the pitch-side screens for a review.

Oliver studied the slow-motion replays and upgraded it to a red card. Off went Thiago, smiling wryly and shaking his head, dismissed for standing his ground and being goaded into a reaction.

He will miss games against Everton, Manchester United and Arsenal.

Opinions of Oliver in the away end did not improve when he gave a penalty for a shirt pull by 5ft 7in Keane Lewis-Potter which somehow sent 6ft 4in Luka Vuskovic somersaulting to the turf.

Vuskovic is already a favourite at the Amex Stadium and it is easy to forget he is only 19. He dominates in the air and reads the game like a seasoned central defender.

And after ten games he is ten points better off than those he left behind at Tottenham.

The Croatia international cannot be looking forward to yet another encounter with England. The two nations meet at Wembley on Thursday. England have put 11 past them in two games this year.

On Saturday, AC Milan will host Inter at San Siro for the first Derby della Madonnina of the season. It's a clash between two of the most important teams in Europe and the first derby for Portuguese coach Ruben Amorim, who joined AC Milan in the summer after leaving Manchester United in January. The two clubs will play at the iconic Italian arena, but on Thursday they unveiled plans for the new stadium that will replace San Siro, which both clubs currently share. The new San Siro will be named Generali Stadium after Italian insurer Generali acquired the naming rights in a deal worth €650 million ($725 million) over 20 years.

The project is a "71,500-seat stadium designed around one of football's most iconic atmospheres, setting a new standard for the live fan experience," according to the clubs. A bold architectural vision by Foster + Partners and MANICA, bringing together Lord Norman Foster and David Manica, the two architects who previously worked on the design of London's Wembley Stadium. The new arena will feature a striking X-frame structure and a sweeping double-curved roof, conceived to become Milan's next landmark. The stadium is a "defining investment" by RedBird and Oaktree, the owners of AC Milan and Inter, respectively, to "strengthen sporting competitiveness, unlock future growth and help shape the next era of Italian football." Two seating tiers form a continuous 360-degree bowl, creating exceptional sightlines and an immersive connection between fans and pitch. At either end, the Curvas rise as single, steep walls of support, drawn forward toward the field of play with seating inclinations of up to 37 degrees to amplify both atmosphere and visual impact. At the heart of the design is a distinctive structural form, whose powerful rhythm recalls both the legacy of Italian engineering and the intricate craftsmanship of the Duomo di Milano.

#1167. Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he said. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the plan. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

“As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the plan disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

If they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight new signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

This is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.

Everton had the lead and it was so easy and straightforward. They waited for Newcastle to give the ball away and then broke at speed. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was superb and forced a fingertip save from Hornicek. From the resulting corner, Hornicek was needed again to keep out Jake O’Brien’s header.

Newcastle tried to gain some momentum and finally created a chance. Harvey Barnes curled a cross to the far post. It bounced awkwardly but Anthony Elanga somehow failed to bundle it across the line.

“Now it is about taking that frustration into motivation for Monday and having that approach for the rematch,” Jaissle said. “We take it as a long-term journey, and our approach is to make progress, to see improvements. Now it is time to learn fast out of the mistakes that we just did. [There are] other phases where we can already see that we improved and this is something we can count on, we can build on, the good part. But football is also in the end about results so you need to avoid these simple mistakes.”

Everton, who have not won in the league since a 1-0 victory over Ipswich back in September, begin the night in 14th but, like Newcastle, could rise to seventh with a win. Jack Grealish was left out of Everton’s squad for that League Cup victory because of an unauthorised absence from training and the 31-year-old is not expected to be involved tonight.
