#1042. Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's  unfair trade practices.

In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.

Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue.

Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means."

China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction."

Before the COVID pandemic, the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent.

Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.

Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking, precision engineering and chemicals industries.

German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.

Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures.

In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.

"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."

Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:

"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.

According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.

While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.

The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.

Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."

Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.

Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report.

Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.

Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.

Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.

MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.

This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.

"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

#1041. Alessia Russo inspires struggling Arsenal to rare WSL win

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

England international Russo earned Arsenal just a third WSL win of the season against Liverpool, while Charlton remain without a point and London City Lionesses bounced back from last week’s disappointment.

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Alessia Russo struck twice in the first half as Arsenal beat Liverpool 2-1 at Anfield for only their third Women’s Super League win of the season.

Russo opened the scoring early and then headed what proved to be the winner just before half-time, rising highest inside the box to meet Lisa Baum’s delivery and nod past Khiara Keating.

Beata Olsson had earlier levelled the score for struggling Liverpool, netting in the 15th minute, but the Gunners secured a priceless three points.

The result lifts Renee Slegers’ side to sixth in the table, although a 12-point gap remains to champions and league leaders Manchester City.

Elsewehere, Julia Zigiotti Olme’s second-half goal gave Manchester United a 1-0 victory over Aston Villa – a first win in three WSL matches for the Red Devils.

Hinata Miyazawa hit the bar in a first half United dominated but they had to wait until 17 minutes from time before Zigiotti Olme nodded in the vital goal.

Bethany England scored in the last minute to earn Crystal Palace a vital 3-2 win over fellow strugglers Charlton, who remain without a point at the bottom of the table.

Lexi Lloyd-Smith had given the hosts a 57th-minute lead before the Addicks hit back with two quick goals through Elisha N’Dow and Leah Davidson and looked on course for their first points of the campaign.

But Aimee Everett got the Eagles back on level terms in the 81st minute and England broke the hearts of their south London rivals at the death.

Third-placed London City Lionesses bounced back from last weekend’s loss to Manchester City with a 4-1 victory over Birmingham.

Early goals from Poppy Pattinson and Delphine Cascarino put the Lionesses in control before Oceane Hurtre pulled Birmingham back into the game just after half-time but Grace Geyoro and 127-cap France international Kadidiatou Diani made sure of the points.

Tottenham’s fine form continued as two goals in three minutes from Signe Gaupset and Olivia Holdt earned them a 2-1 victory over Brighton.

Brighton had taken a very early lead through Fran Kirby but Gauspest and Holdt did enough to lift Spurs up to fourth.

#1039. Xabi Alonso disgusted after Chelsea bullied by Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

Enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”

On where Chelsea stand ahead of the international break...

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”

They cannot make anything of set piece and Sunderland have the three points - it wasn’t pretty but they needed the three points and edged the contest.

Questions will be asked of Chelsea now, they were bullied in the first-half and weren’t able to create anything in the second.

Chelsea with the ball inside the Sunderland half. The visitors bring Rogers down and Chelsea have a free-kick. Last-chance sallon for the west Londoners...

Sunderland have a throw inside the Chelsea half - this is about game management for the side in dire need of a win now...

Angulo nrings down his man after a poor pass from Sadiki. The visitors with a free-kick inside their own half.

Emegha drifts past Mukiele before he feels the full force of a Luke O’Nein tackle. It looks as though he gets the ball but the ref awards the free-kick. It’s in the final third, can Chelsea create anything from this?

In short ‘yes’, Estevao delivers a peach of a ball and Welbeck gets on the end of it. BUT his header is over, when it seemed easier to hit the target.

Sunderland in Chelsea half, they’re looking for a free-kick as Angulo goes down. The referee isn’t having any of it...

Sunderland break at pace (only the second time this half) Isador finds Talbi who is free before cutting inside and unleashing a shot from outside the box. It’s just wide, don’t think it was too far away though.

Talbi is off for Angulo, Rigg on for Le Fee for Sunderland, and for Chelsea, Henderson makes way for Emegha.

For all their possession this half Chelsea have not forced Roefs into a meaningful save. The west Londoners are again dominating possession in and near the hinterland of the Sunderland box, but it’s all a bit after you Claude and ultimately Roefs gladly picks up an anaemic cross. That sums up Chelsea as an attacking force today.

Chelsea corner after Geovany Quenda gets in a shot from the left-side of the area that gets a tiny hint of a deflection. Roefs punches away the set-piece and Sunderland breathe a sigh of relief.

Better from Sunderland, there are spaces in behind Chelsea as the visitors go in search of the equaliser and over the past few minutes the hosts have found them.

Lovely ball from Reinildo finds Sadiki in space on the left, they keep the ball brilliantly before Le Fee plays in Isador, it’s a one-on-one and all the Frenchman has to do it dink it over the on-rushing keeper. He goes low, however, and Penders makes a fine save - that was the game for Sunderland there...Penders has kept Chelsea in this.

Brobbey may have been tiring but without him Sunderland cannot keep the ball. Sadiki earns a free-kick which takes a bit of pressure off the hosts.

Palmer pulls back for Gusto whose dinky, cheeky chip tries to find Roefs off his line. He doesn’t succeed and the Dutch goalkeeper claims with ease.

Chelsea still seeing plenty of the ball, Sunderland may well be tiring. It’s hard to keep up that intensity for 90 minutes, hence Isador on for Brobbey, but they are struggling to keep the ball at the moment.

The first half was lively and entertaining, this half has been lively and lacking in anything that could be remotely described as a spectacle...

Rogers tries to find Palmer, but the ball is too long and Roefs gobbles up with ease.

Meanwhile, Hume looks injured and Chelsea do not give the ball back after Sunderland kicked it off. You won’t be shocked to hear that the home fans are not happy with that...

Change for Sunderland, Brobbey off for Isador. The Dutchman has been brilliant today, he might have scored a couple of goals, but despite not finding the back of the net he has proved a handful for the Chelsea backline. I would have kept him on for longer...

Chelsea looking better this half, they’re seeing plenty of the ball but have not had a shot on goal since the break. In fact there have only been two touches in either box this 45...Sunderland won’t mind that at 1-0.

ON - Welbeck and GustoOFF - Neto and Palestra

So Alonso has opted for a physical presence up front.

No sooner had I pressed send on that last post than Chelsea break through the middle but some great last-ditch defending from Muenier prevents Estevao from getting a shot at goal.

Chelsea haven’t been able to play through Sunderland and you think they’d need to bring on a physical presence up front if that’s to change.

Another chance for Sunderland - they break down the right before Hume sends in a low ball to the penalty box, it’s met first time by Le Fee, I think, and Penders saves low to his right. To state the obvious, the hosts would love a second to give them a deserved cushion. As I typed that last but the linesman has his flag up, it wouldn’t have counted, promising signs nonetheless.

Pressure from Sunderland. A good bit of possession ends with Mukiele swinging in a lovely cross from the right which Chelsea are forced to head clear for a corner. Nothing results from the set piece, but things still looking promising for Sunderland who look as energetic and ‘at it’ as they did in the first half.

Rogers picks up the ball in the middle just inside the Sunderland half and is immediately pick-pocketed by one of three Sunderland players. The Chelsea men have not been allowed to settle when they have a sniff of a mini counter.

Good, feisty opening to this half, Chelsea look more up for it, though to be fair they couldn’t look any more insipid than they did in the first 45. Meanwhile, Brobbey shoves Lavia and earns a yellow. Think that’s three yellows for the hosts now.

It is going to be fascinating to see how a team with well known - and long standing - disciplinary issues copes with a pressurised pursuit of an equaliser. There have already been a couple of flash points that Chelsea’s players have reacted to and it wouldn’t be the wildest thing to predict referee Jarred Gillett brandishing a red card before the end of the game. Watch it unfold with interest.

Brobbey lays the ball off for Meunier in the final third, it’s asking a lot of the Belgian but his compounds the Dutchman’s error with one of his own - stretching for the ball and taking out Caicedo. Something for which he earns a needless yellow card.

There’s a bit of argy bargy on the pitch, not sure what started that but the referee Jarred Gillett has to have a word with several players. All a bit of handbags really.

They’re back under way on the banks of the Wear. Chelsea have been insipid and you imagine they won’t be as bed these next 45 minutes. Can Sunderland play with the same aggression and energy? We’re about to find out.

Changes Estevao on for Colwill, interesting substitution to say the least...

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The half ends with an audacious attempt at goal from Rogers, a full 40 yards out from a free kick. It’s catching practice for Roefs and that sums up Chelsea as an attacking force in the first 45. Sunderland are well worth their lead.

Rogers has a shot-cum-cross from the left and it sails high, wide and not so handsome. He’s been on the periphery this half, as has Palmer and that explains as much as anything why they are behind. Sunderland have cut out the supply to him and Roefs has had little to do as a result.

Approaching half-time and save for the contentious VAR call when he wanted a penalty, Cole Palmer has done absolutely nothing. The talk of him being in the England squad, on this evidence, is for the birds. Sunderland are full value for their half-time lead. Chelsea, like Palmer, have been absolutely insipid.

There will be five minutes added time in this first half.

Something I’ve not written much this half ‘chance for Chelsea’. Neto works a bit of space in the inside-right channel outside the box, but his shot is easily saved by Roefs.

Talbi attacks down the left but cuts in when he would have been better served going wide.

Chelsea have seen plenty of the ball but they’ve been way too slow and cumbersome with it. It’s been in front of the Sunderland back lines and easy to defend against. The hosts are letting the visitors have the ball wide and with Neto in the middle, it’s been too easy for Le Bris’s men.

Brobbey wants the ball at every opportunity and Sunderland would be well advised to give it to him. Colwill is has his hands full.

Sunderland have kept the aggression and energy throughout the half - and kept Chelsea quiet as a result. As I type that the hosts give Lavia too much room 25 yards out and his shot is well wide of the left-hand post.

The lead is no more than Sunderland deserve and that means, as the table stands, Manchester United are bottom of the Premier League. Fair play to Enzo Le Fee for keeping his nerve in a pressure situation. Sunderland needed him to be cool.

They’ve deserved that, they’ve been the better side and are well worth the lead. Le Fee sends Penders the wrong way, burying the ball into the bottom left corner.

Brobbey has been a handful (as he always is) and Colwill brings the BIG (yes, caps lock and bold are necessary) Dutchman down in the box. It looks as though it was six of one and hald a dozen of the other, but the spotkick stands.

Ahoka has impressed since coming on, his nifty footwork helps win Sunderland a throw in the final third. Mukiele has a big thrown on him but it does not result in a chance. Still, this is good from the hosts and Chelsea are second best at the moment. They were in the first half against United last week, and ended up winning so...

Another chance for Sunderland as Brobbey bullies Colwill on the halfway line before driving at Fofana. He gets to the edge of the area, beats the Chelsea defender before his shot goes wide. The last touch took him too wide, but again, promising signs for the hosts.

Early days this, of course, but Sunderland absolutely do not look like a team that is currently the worst in the Premier League. They should have the lead here but Brian Brobbey’s miss from six yards is indicative of how things have been going.

Sunderland are being aggressive, they need to be and it’s a contrast from the previous month. With that approach, however, comes risks and Mukiele gives away a free-kick inside his own half. Luckily for him, nothing comes from the set-piece.

First chance of the game for Chelsea and, as with Brobbey 10 minutes ago, it should have found the back of the net. Rogers is the culprit - he sends his header wide of the right post after a grade-A cross from Palestra.

One-all in terms of great chances...but the score remains 0-0.

Palmer is bundled over on the outskirts of the area and he and Chelsea players appeal for something - could be a free-kick of penalty...the referee is having nothing of it. The replay suggests he may well have been hard done by but VAR also is having nothing of it...it was a foul as none of the marauding Sunderland players, O’Nien among them (obviously), got the ball and most definitely got Palmer...think the hosts got away with that one.

Yellow card for Ahoka for a foul on Caicado, he may need to walk a tightrope for the rest of the match. But it’s an illustration of the energy and purpose with which Sunderland have approached this match.

Sunderland have looked the better side so far and have had the better chances.

Better from Chelsea in the sense that they controlled the game for two minutes. Lots of good, neat passing but no end product, it’s all in front of a composed Sunderland defence.

Another good chance for Sunderland and once again Talbi proves his worth. He cuts back onto his right and delivers a peach of a cross from the left. Brobbey gets in front of his man and all he has to do is hit the target...alas his first-time shot goes wide. That should be 1-0 to the hosts who are the better side at the moment.

Good from Sunderland who look so much more energetic than at any point during their previous few matches. Ahoka does well in the middle before freeing Talbi down the left. The Moroccan gets in a cross and Le Fee’s shot is blocked. Promising signs for the hosts.

What a blow this is for Regis Le Bris. Less than two minutes gone and Granit Xhaka is having to leave the pitch with an obvious injury. Some fans around the press box booed Xhaka as he was hobbling off - is that a hangover from his attempts to move to Chelsea? - but on afternoon when Le Bris needed everything to go his way, he’s already on the back foot.

Neto is in the Sunderland half but three Sunderland players snap at his heels like a hyperactive dog after a bone. Chelsea haven’t been allowed to settle yet. Plenty of time to go though...

Sunderland are looking to find Brobbey at every opportunity, but Chelsea’s backline intercept well. Nothing of note created so far, but the hosts are on the front foot, which is what they and the fans needed.

Sunderland attack down the right with Meunier, nothing comes of it but the hosts look as though they mean business here. A minute later Sadiki and Brobbey nearly combine to create something. Close but no cigar...

Bad news for Sunderland, Xhaka is down and it looks as though he may well have to come off...oh dear. While he’s not been at his best this season he’s still the man the side looks towards for inspiration (an boy do they need that is dollops today...)...and, indeed he is forced off. Ahoka, who is highly rated but raw replaces him. The Congolese player now has a big chance to make a name for himself.

Chelsea with the early possession, but they go backwards and the hosts are up and at them with the press and the visitors have to go back to Penders in goal.

They’re under way at the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in their famous red and white and Chelsea in their away outfit of black shirts and shorts and yelow socks.

As the Stadium of Light remembers all those who lost their lives in war.

The Last Post is played and the minute’s silence is impeccably observed.

Warming-up in our Remembrance shirt ❤️ https://t.co/aTB8sfdLKP

And we’re moments away from kick-off in the North East.

This is a big afternoon for both teams. It will be an emotional one, too, for Jordan Henderson, who started his career at Sunderland many years ago. Xabi Alonso has confirmed he has been picked because of the quality he provides, rather than any sentimental value, and Regis Le Bris revealed ahead of the fixture he tried to bring the England international home during the summer window, when Chelsea attempted to sign Granit Xhaka.

“Jordan is a great player, first of all,” said Le Bris. “For the connection with the club, it’s not my part. It was with Flo [Ghisolfi, director of football] and Kyril [Louis-Dreyfus, the Sunderland owner], they had conversations.

“I thought that it could have been a good signing for the club, a good symbol, a great player, a great leader. But the market is the market.”

Has just said that Sunderland, and in particular Brian Brobbey, can ‘get at’ the Chelsea defence of Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria. I am not sure he has seen much of the Sunderland attack this year, but Brobbey is a handful for any defence.

“We have to stay consistent and true to our identity. It’s always difficult to predict what the other side does but you have to focus on yourself and connect with the fans and impose our ideas.”

On whether they can get a result today...

“I hope so... I see the players every day, they care and sometime its hard to understand the unforced errors.”

“He’s loved by fans and team, so we know the situation at beginning of season. He is an important player for us and didn’t start for various reasons, but has qualities run in behind and finish - he’s excited worked and has worked hard.”

I mentioned earlier that Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season. But the manner of the victories revealed more than the scorelines. In both matches, especially the second, the west Londoners looked somewhat lightweight and easily bullied.

This season Xabi Alonso has been determined to ensure that that is not the case this season.

In the land of the Premier League giants, Chelsea have been on the small side in recent seasons. But they are no longer being looked down upon and are finally showing signs of being capable of going toe-to-toe physically with opponents.

Sunday’s opponents Sunderland ran Chelsea off the park twice last season. Only once, in the 36th Premier League game of the campaign against Liverpool, did Chelsea cover more distance than their opposition.

Here’s Matt Law’s article on Why Chelsea have gone from pint-sized players to taller trees...

SUNDERLAND XI TO FACE CHELSEA: Roefs, Meunier, Mukiele, O’Nein, Reinildo, Xhaka, Hume, Le Fee, Talbi, Brobbey.

Subs: Ellborg, Danso, Methalie, Rigg, Tutierov, Ahoka, Fofana, Angulo, Isador

Regis Le Bris makes two changes from the sorry defeat at Coventry City. Nordi Mukiele returns to the centre of defence and there’s a start for Chemsdine Talbi  – Chris Rigg and Nilson Angulo are the ones to make way.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE SUNDERLAND: Penders, Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria, Henderson, Lavia, Caicedo, Neto, Palmer, Rogers.

Subs: Sharman-Lowe, Gusto, Anselmino, Nicoll-Jazuli, Barco, Quenda, Estevao, Welbeck, Emegha.

Xabi Alonso also makes two changes – Pep Chavarria and Jordan Henderson start today. Estevao Willian drops to the bench while Josh Acheampong is a somewhat surprise absence the 20.

Goalkeeper Mike Penders continues in goal with Emiliano Martinez deemed not ready to return having fractured his jaw against Everton.

That Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season.

A last-minute winner from Chemsdine Talbi grabbed the points at Stamford Bridge, before Sunderland won 2-1, without breaking sweat, at the Stadium of Light on the last day of the campaign.

Those victories, and the manner of them, underlined what a season it was for Regis Le Bris’s men. How they wish this campaign started as that one ended.

RLB's XI to take on Chelsea! 📝👊 #SUNCHE https://t.co/1XWyHk0x56

Your Chelsea side today! ✔️ #CFC | #SUNCHE https://t.co/ciaILJeAuu

For Sunderland that argument is easy to make – they are bottom of the Premier League, are without a win since August and for morale, if nothing else need at least a point, though three is really what the doctor orders.

For Chelsea – fourth in the table and with three wins in their past four league outings – the argument that this is a must-win game is harder to make, but bear with me here...

Facing a Sunderland team who are suffering from the worst of both worlds – blunt in attack and pitiful in defence (what a difference from last season...) and have proven all too easy to beat (as their 2-0 home defeat Zagreb illustrated on Thursday) – the west Londoners are expected to win. Fail to return to the capital with the three points and there will once again be question marks over Xabi Alonso’s side. They are flaky and flashy in equal measure, able to play and win well in spurts, but once again unable to mount sustained pressure needed for a title challenge and forced to battle it out for the hope of a top-four spot at best. Those will be the arguments raised should they not win this afternoon.

The hosts doubtless wish that their ‘issues’ were as golden as today’s opposition. For Trai Hume, who scored in this fixture last season, the Sunderland players are at fault for the sorry start to the season and he wants to put right the wrongs so far, starting today.

“I couldn’t tell you what’s changed. We thought we’d addressed it after the Leeds game, where we were aggressive, strong, but we go out there tonight and see the old habits of the start of the season. Everything’s a bit laboured, and it’s something the staff can’t fix, it’s on us as players,” Hume said.

“We’re still together as a club, as a team. I think the run of form we’re on, it would be easy to think we’re not, but we are. We are really upset with how we’ve been playing, and the results don’t lie. We haven’t been good enough and we know that. We have to address that.”

#1038. Wirtz breaks goalscoring duck as Liverpool send Palace boss closer to exit door

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Crystal Palace 1-3 Liverpool: Andoni Iraola’s side bounced back from two defeats on the spin but Palace, bottom of the table after 10 games, could now be forced to make a change in the dugout

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

For Andoni Iraola, at the end of a week of vexation following two avoidable one-goal defeats, this was just what the doctor ordered. On a cool November day, a comfortable margin of victory in second gear in South London halted Liverpool’s two-game losing run heading into the internationals and catapulted them back into the top-four, nine points off leaders Arsenal.

Even Florian Wirtz, Liverpool’s ultimate attacking fall guy over the last 15 months, netted a much-needed first Premier League goal of the season. Off a Bradley Barcola assist, too. Here at Selhurst, amid a forward quartet made up of just shy of £400m worth of transfer fees, there were more positive sprinklings of encouragement. And when Alexander Isak, who it should be said is second in the race for the golden boot with seven league goals, smashed the ball home on the cusp of 90 minutes, the three points were safe and heading back up to the north-west.

That said, this was all against a Crystal Palace side – and a manager in beleaguered Frenchman Pierre Sage – who by the end looked out of ideas and inspiration. No head coach has lost his job in the Premier League this season – yet – but the Eagles are now rooted to the bottom of the table after 10 games with just two wins to their name. Could a change be in the offing from Palace chairman Steve Parish, a man who does tend to afford managers time to put things right? We’ll find out soon enough.

Yet what will frustrate Sage the most on this occasion is that, until Liverpool’s second just after half-time, Palace were well in this match. But the team that has scored the second-fewest goals in the division (ten) were punished here for failing to take their chances in the first-half.

But a week on from failing to have a single shot on target against Arsenal, it took 20 seconds for Liverpool to find their range here as Mac Allister gave Dean Henderson an early test. The diminutive 5’9” midfielder, curiously effective from set pieces, went closer after 10 minutes, heading into the side netting from Dominik Szoboszlai’s free-kick. It was a warning and routine that Palace would not heed.

Yet after the first 15 minutes, Palace were the team on the ascendancy. Yeremy Pino’s neat swivel and shot crashed off the crossbar while Jogen Strand Larsen, in for the suspended Jean-Philippe Mateta, saw a dinked finish ruled out for offside, albeit correctly so.

And when Daichi Kamada gave Barcola a lesson in back-post volleys with a punchy effort kept out by Alisson, it was somewhat against the run of play when Mac Allister’s opener arrived.

Iraola had spoken in the build-up about his team perhaps being “too honest” as a statistic this week did the rounds: while Liverpool have conceded the most fouls in the Premier League, only three sides have won fewer fouls. But it pays to be shrewd. After Cody Gakpo won a questionably-given foul off Jefferson Lerma, Szoboszlai’s near-post free-kick was once again met by Mac Allister, who glanced sweetly home for his fifth goal of the season, equalling his tally from the last campaign.

His provocative celebration in front of the Holmesdale End only added to the home crowd's fury. “One-nil to the referee,” they sang at official Tony Harrington at the interval.

The Reds were, however, fortunate to be ahead at half-time. Their goal was under siege before the interval, with Quinten Timber and Adam Wharton forcing good saves out of Alisson. Palace’s momentum was stymied by the interval though and when Barcola’s square ball after a surge down the right found Wirtz, the German found the attribute he so often has been accused of lacking since his £105m arrival on these shores: composure. Stroking the ball beyond Henderson, it is just his sixth Premier League goal since arriving from Bayer Leverkusen last summer.

But even in the closing stages, Palace carved out decent opportunities. Pino somehow squandered a one-on-one opportunity with the goal gaping and substitute Eddie Nketiah poked over from close range. It was indicative of Palace’s fortunes: neat build-up, a large intake of breath in the box before failing to find the back of the net.

And when Isak put the icing on the cake, set up by Wirtz in the box and coolly cutting inside before lashing home past Henderson, Sage had the look of a man on the brink on the touchline. Even Milos Kerkez’s brainless foul on Dario Osorio in stoppage time, clattering the Palace substitute’s head in the box, which resulted in Nketiah’s consolation penalty and a needless ruining of Alisson’s clean sheet, could not brighten the Palace mood. Now, ahead of a two-week pause in action, the question for Parish is: will he stick or twist?

#1035. Aston Villa boss Unai Emery storms down the tunnel after last-gasp Man United equaliser

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

United trailed 4-2 in injury time at Old Trafford but rescued a point with a 4-4 draw and Villa boss Emery stormed down the tunnel after the goal

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery appeared to storm off down the tunnel after Manchester United grabbed a last-gasp equaliser against his side to seal a remarkable 4-4 draw in one of the most chaotic Premier League games of the season.

United looked set for defeat as they trailed 4-2 in the second minute of injury-time at Old Trafford before Joshua Zirkzee gave them a sliver of hope by pulling one back and Patrick Dorgu headed home an incredible equaliser in the 96th minute.

That proved to be the final straw for Emery, who immediately stormed off down the tunnel without even waiting for the VAR check confirming the goal and before the full-time whistle blew for the end of the match.

In his post-match interview with Sky Sports, Emery suggested he simply left because United scored so late that he thought the match was essentially over.

Emery had already watched his side squander a 2-0 lead after the perfect start for the visiting Villans, with Alysson and Nicolas Jackson both finding the net inside the first five minutes.

That advantage didn’t last long as Matheus Cunha was fouled in the box by Boubacar Kamara and Bruno Fernandes stepped up to pull one back, sparking a period of constant pressure that continued until Youri Tielemans scored his first United goal to equalise against his former club before half-time.

Yet the hosts unravelled again however, as Villa scored twice in seven minutes after the restart, with John McGinn netting from the penalty spot after Diogo Dalot fouled Alysson and Leon Goretzka tapping in after more woeful defending from United.

At that point, Emery must have assumed his team would get over the line but they collapsed again with Zirkzee first pulling one back in the 92nd minute before Dorgu rose highest on 96 minutes to head into an empty net after Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki came off his line and failed to get the ball.

That result – combined with their incredible comeback victory against Roma in midweek – may just have saved Michael Carrick’s job, although his United side still head into this international break in the Premier League’s bottom three, lying 18th in the table.

Meanwhile, Villa’s rollercoaster start to the campaign means they are in 10th, although if they had held on for victory, they would have moved up to eighth.

#1033. The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech

Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smartwatches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of hidden treasure.

From mini fans and the cheap chargers to smartwatches bought as part of a New Year's health kick, some 44% of Europeans own at least six "fast-tech" gadgets. And more than half say they keep unused and broken e-waste items languishing at home or throw them in the regular trash instead of recycling.

That's according to a new report by Brussels-based e-waste association WEEE Forum. It describes fast tech, which is booming, as charging and lighting devices under €10 (circa $11), high-tech items like power banks and fitness trackers, and gadgets and lifestyle appliances like cheap mini blenders and fans, as well as single-use electronic vapes.

"So, these electronics are a bit like fast fashion," Magdalena Charytanowicz, WEEE Forum's Communication Manager, told DW.

Nearly 40% of buyers recalled discarding a fast-tech item without using it at all or within a month of buying it, and nearly 60% said they had used a product for no longer than six months. Yet the vast majority of respondents were generally satisfied with their gadgets despite short-lived functionality.

This suggests consumers accept the "fast-tech bargain" of poor quality that "does the job for a while" and is easily replaced — similar to fast fashion — according to the report.

About 62 million tons of electronics are discarded worldwide annually. "That's the Great Wall of China of e-waste that is produced every year," noted Charytanowicz, adding that the figure is set to grow to 82 million by 2030.

In Europe, roughly 40% of electronic waste is recycled, yet the rate worldwide is just 17%. This means valuable materials are lost, while electronic waste ends up polluting the environment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2022, a million tons of critical raw materials were embedded in the 10.7 million tons of e-waste generated across Europe, including manganese, gold, copper and aluminum.

These materials are at "the center of geopolitical tensions," Charytanowicz said, referring to escalating global tensions over access to rare earths and other critical minerals.

"Even the smallest" devices are worth recycling if they contain a circuit board or battery, she said.

Groups like WEEE Forum say more awareness raising is needed on how to dispose of cheap electronic devices, and that recycling should be made as easy as possible.

But the best way to reduce a product's environmental impact is to extend its lifespan through better design and repair, as recycling raw materials is energy intensive.

Charytonawicz said clearer, harmonized EU rules now under consideration could help improve e-waste collection. The bloc's 20-year-old directive is "not really adapted to the changing reality," she said.

Another growing area of e-waste is digital healthcare. While devices such as diabetes sensors and blood pressure monitors are "transforming healthcare," many are designed to be disposable.

A study published in Nature in December 2025 found sales of wearable healthcare electronics, for example, could reach 2 billion devices annually by 2050, and generate a million tons of e-waste.

Jeremy Faludi, associate professor of sustainable design engineering at TU Delft in the Netherlands, says making health tech — particularly digital devices used in, or issued by hospitals — recyclable or reusable comes with some "much bigger challenges" than normal electronics.

That's in part due to the potential for patient contamination, particularly with digital surgical devices that come into contact with blood or other bodily fluids.

"The way that a lot of things are designed now, you can't recover the stuff because it can't be easily sterilized without the electronics," said Faludi.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He worked on the Digital Health in Circular Economy (DiCE) project, an EU-funded initiative, to help redesign digital healthcare devices to "recover critical materials and reduce environmental impacts without compromising patient safety."

A modular design, for example, allows electronic components to be separated from the parts that need to be replaced between patients, making devices easier to reuse.

The four-year DiCE project, which included citizens, hospitals and manufacturers across nine EU countries, found reusable ECG cables — which connect patients to heart-monitoring equipment — cut environmental impacts by up to 81-94%, for example. The sets are usually designed for single use.

Rules around medical waste can also make reuse and recycling more difficult, particularly when requirements differ between countries and often come down to perceived rather than actual risk, Faludi added. He says some 85% of hospital trash is not infectious but everything ends up in the same bins. Better sorting as well as EU-wide regulations around treating non-infectious hospital waste would help here.

Like with other tech, consumer health devices such as blood pressure and glucose monitors often risk being forgotten in drawers or ending up in the wrong waste, simply because people do not know how to dispose of them, said Charytanowicz of WEEE Forum, which is also involved in DiCE.

Pilot schemes in Belgium, Spain and Slovenia that offered free postal returns and collection machines in public places found that more than 60% of people were willing to return unwanted devices if it was a straightforward process.

"What's really important is the convenience so that it can be integrated in your daily routines," said Charytanowicz, adding that "nudges" such as messages that recycling a device could help the health of another person motivate people to "do the right thing."

#1032. Michael Carrick has painfully awkward exchange with interviewer over Man United future

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Carrick appeared to be unimpressed by questioning from Sky Sports after United’s remarkable 4-4 draw with Aston Villa as he gave a series of terse responses

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick endured an awkward end to a post-match interview as he had an excruciating exchange about his future as Manchester United manager.

Carrick had just watched his United side fight back from 4-2 down in injury time to snatch the unlikeliest of 4-4 draws with Aston Villa, having earlier come back from being 2-0 behind inside five minutes.

It was a real mixed display from the Red Devils, who showed plenty of heart and character but had put themselves in bad positions due to consistently disastrous defending.

The result – combined with their incredible comeback victory against Roma in midweek – has probably saved Carrick’s job, although his United side still head into this international break in the Premier League’s bottom three, lying 18th in the table.

His long-term future appears to very much still be up in the air and his post-match interview on Sky Sports with reporter Patrick Davison was an awkward watch.

Carrick firstly bristled slightly when asked if United are looking at a relegation fight, saying: “No, we’re in November. I don’t like this situation we’re in, I don’t like the results we’ve had but we can definitely do something about it.”

From there, things got worse, as Davison asked a lengthy question suggesting there were clearly going to be conversations about his future during the international break over the next couple of weeks, to which Carrick simply responded: "Is there?"

When it was suggested that one would assume so, Carrick tersely said: “Would you?” and when he was pushed for what he thought about his situation, the Man United boss said to Davison: “You’re telling me, what do you think”.

After that, the interviewer specified that he wanted to know what Carrick expected to happen in the next couple of weeks and he then gave a longer answer admitting that it wasn’t a good situation, the team haven’t won enough games but that he expects to move forward and keep working on the things they’ve been working on until this point.

Back in the Sky Sports studio, pundit Roy Keane was asked for his thoughts on the interview as a whole and the former Man United midfielder compared the current boss to a politician.

He said: “It’s obviously difficult for the manager, he’s under pressure no doubt. He talks a lot but doesn’t say much – maybe that’s a tactic. He’s like a politician.

“He’s clearly under pressure and says he knows there are things to work on but he better get moving on that... This is their worst start in however many years.”

Keane was also critical of United’s “dreadful” defending, although he praised the heart they showed to twice come back from two goals behind.

He added: “I think we’ve said previously there have been question marks over this team but they’re showing a bit of fight, a bit of desire and, as bad as the game was from a footballing point of view, they kept going to the end.

“So, on the one hand, you say dreadful to give up four goals at home, but they kept going, so we have to give them a little bit of praise.

“In terms of the bigger picture, it’s that rollercoaster of watching United. Some bits were so, so bad. Defensively the way it started, the start of the second half, but they found a way to get a point in a game where they looked dead and buried.

“Still nowhere near good enough to try and get towards the middle of the table.”

The Leicester City manager’s reputation may never recover if his side lose to non-League Oxford City tonight

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As night falls this evening, the Leicester City team coach will edge through the rush-hour traffic on Marsh Lane and turn left through the unassuming entrance to Court Place Farm.

It will make its way along the narrow lane to the MGroup Stadium, where manager Russell Martin and his players will disembark with the sole intention of avoiding FA Cup humiliation against sixth-tier Oxford City.

When they board the coach again a few hours later, it will be with either relief or embarrassment, depending on whether they suffer a giant-killing that would make national and potentially international headlines. For Martin, it would be a defeat he may never be able to shake off.

That Leicester team coach has travelled to English football’s most famous stadiums, from Anfield to Wembley.

But its journey from the East Midlands to Oxfordshire for this FA Cup first round tie is a sign of how far the Foxes have fallen, just five years after lifting the trophy and only 10 years after winning the Premier League.

Martin’s managerial career - or perhaps more accurately, his reputation - has experienced a similarly sharp decline.

He was aged just 33 when he became MK Dons head coach in November 2019, when he was still on the club’s playing staff. In 2020/21, his only full season, the League One team boasted the third-highest possession percentage per game in Europe - behind only Manchester City and Barcelona - and scored a goal against Gillingham following a 56-pass move, a British record.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

MK ended the campaign 13th, but Swansea City had seen enough to make Martin their manager. After solid but unspectacular finishes of 15th and 10th in the Championship, he moved to newly-relegated Southampton in summer 2023.

After a slow start, he led Saints to promotion back to the Premier League, via a club-record 25-game unbeaten run and a play-off final victory over Leeds United. It emerged this week that Martin was even earmarked as a future Manchester United manager by the club’s director of football, Jason Wilcox.

His stock had never been higher, but within six months it had crashed. Martin became a top-flight manager by favouring a possession-based style, but his refusal to change his approach became a stick to beat him with as Southampton floundered. He was sacked in December 2024 with Saints rock-bottom, having claimed just five points from 16 games.

Somehow, it got worse. Martin was named Rangers boss in summer 2025 but lasted just 123 days - the shortest stint by a permanent manager in the club’s history - after the fans turned on him amid poor results and some PR disasters.

It was why there was widespread derision when Leicester appointed the 40-year-old in June, as they prepared for life in League One following successive relegations. The jeers grew louder after some embarrassing early-season defeats, most notably a 4-0 thrashing by Oxford United at the King Power Stadium.

Fast forward to the present day and another clash with a team from Oxford, and Martin has won just 15 out of 53 games since leading Southampton to promotion. That being said, he is currently on his best run of form in that time, with Leicester taking 10 points from their past five matches.

The problem is that Martin has become such a lightning rod for criticism that whenever the Foxes drop points, the knives come out. Here are some of the comments under the club’s posts on X after the Foxes twice let slip a lead to draw 2-2 at home to Stevenage last Saturday:

“Get used to this with that clown as manager.”

“Whilst he remains in charge we remain in League One. His team selections, tactics, subs all questionable. As soon as we come up against anyone half decent we are found out. Get rid.”

“I want a flexible manager not a one-trick pony.”

“Your possession obsession is causing the team to go back rather than forward too much.”

While X is not always an accurate barometer of public opinion, these comments marked all the squares on the Russell Martin bingo card. To his critics, he is a "clown" and a "one-trick pony" ("fraud" is another popular insult), whose "possession obsession" means his teams are "found out" far too easily.

The latter criticism is certainly valid, as there is no doubt that his tactical inflexibility accelerated his downfall at Southampton and contributed to some of Leicester’s poor results this season.

Equally, the Venn diagram of people who do not like Martin and also hate ‘tippy tappy football’ probably has quite a crowded intersection. For some people, his failures vindicate their belief that a possession-based approach is overrated.

And if Leicester lose to Oxford City live on TV, it will vindicate their belief that Martin is a "clown".

Tonight’s game has all the ingredients of an FA Cup upset: an underperforming giant going to an in-form non-League club (City are second in National League North), who boast several former EFL players including ex-Sheffield Wednesday and Watford winger Fernando Forestieri and former Bristol City and Oxford United striker Matty Taylor.

City’s ground will be full to its 3,500 capacity, with the fans crammed in close to the action. The only thing missing is a playing surface resembling a mudbath, as City have a 3G pitch.

That should allow Leicester to dominate possession, but if they still come up short, well, Martin’s critics will feel they have been proved right.

Alternatively, if the Foxes win with little fuss, maybe the narrative around Martin will start to change. One victory over a non-League side will not move the needle, but you would expect a clown to slip on a banana skin, not calmly pick it up and toss it in the bin.

If Leicester then continue their good form and mount a promotion charge, he might even be praised for reversing his and the Foxes’ decline.

But that is a discussion for another day. Today, Martin must avoid a humiliating defeat from which his reputation may never recover.

James Roberts is a freelance sports journalist working for FourFourTwo and other titles. He started his career at the Oxford Mail, where he covered Oxford United home and away, before becoming a sports sub-editor for various national newspapers.

The former Liverpool left-back had a couple of high-profile fallings-out in his time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Trouble had a way of finding John Arne Riise during his playing days.

He infamously had a run-in with John Carew while on international duty with Norway in 2003, with the Liverpool left-back reportedly getting sparked out by the big striker following an argument Riise started by spitting at Carew's feet.

Then, in February 2007, a ridiculous argument over karaoke led Craig Bellamy to set about Riise with a golf club as the Norwegian lay in his hotel bed after a 'team bonding trip' to Portugal.

Riise reflected to FourFourTwo: "The thing with Carew only happened quickly, and we spoke the same night.

"It shouldn't have happened, but we talked about it the same day and have been friends ever since.

"The thing with Bellamy was more threatening because it was with a golf club.

It sounds stupid, and people think I'm kidding, but he went for my shins. It could have ended my career.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"He was drunk and all over the place mentally, so that was scarier. If I didn't jump out of bed and protect my shins, I would have been done.

"But at the same time, if I met those two one against one, I'd be more scared of Carew than of Bellamy, for sure."

Amusingly, Bellamy and Riise both scored for Liverpool as they beat Barcelona to progress on their way to the 2007 final - and even more bizarrely, that incident with Bellamy went on to play a part in Wrexham's history, of all clubs. No pun intended.

As reported at the time, Bellamy requested that part of his fine should be donated to ailing Wrexham, who were then second-bottom of League Two.

A Wrexham statement later said: "The directors of Wrexham FC would personally like to say a very big thank you on behalf of all our supporters to Wales' own Craig Bellamy for the very generous donation he has made to Wrexham Football Club.

"This has allowed us to bring in three loan players to aid our fight for Football League survival."

Those loan signings Richard Walker (from Port Vale), Michael Proctor (from Hartlepool) and Tony Williams (from Carlisle), ultimately helped Wrexham rise well clear of the drop... though they were ultimately relegated the following season.

#1029. Man United’s unique comeback leaves no one knowing how to feel

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa: Michael Carrick was applauded off as his players rescued an extraordinary draw, even though his side remained 18th in the Premier League and on an eight-game winless run

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As the Manchester United players who had been told they were not fit to wear the shirt, in perhaps the earliest ever airing of that chant in footballing history, celebrated a second ridiculous comeback in five days, the Stretford End launched into a different chorus.

They had told the team they were unworthy of representing them after a mere five minutes, had jeered in damning fashion when the dreadful Diogo Dalot was substituted, had been vitriolic about the Glazer family, Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Jason Wilcox. But United left the pitch in the relegation zone while their supporters serenaded Michael Carrick.

“It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes,” they sang. In one respect, it was hard to believe it was not Sir Alex Ferguson, plucking results from nowhere. In another, it was hard to believe this was not the prelude to a sacking. It may still be.

But Carrick won’t quit. “That’s not going to happen,” he said. “I am quite clear what direction the club needs to go in and we need to win games.” They have only won once in 11 games, one point in three in the Premier League but Carrick is starting to specialise in escapology. Bournemouth had seemed the end for him, Roma looked it when his side were 2-0 down. Aston Villa seemed his valedictory game twice, before two two-goal comebacks.

“Making it hard for ourselves,” said Carrick. That was putting it mildly. Yet his side have twice delivered a show of spirit to salvage something from the brink of humiliation. Ferguson’s most famous comeback was delivered by two substitutes, Teddy Sheringham and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. If Carrick has a lifeline now, it came from two replacements, scorers in Fergie Time, when it seemed time had run out for the latest United manager.

First Patrick Dorgu set up Joshua Zirkzee to halve the deficit. Then Dorgu headed in Bruno Fernandes’ 96th-minute corner. “In extra time conceding two goals is painful,” said Unai Emery. “Today we have lost two points.” Emery headed off for the tunnel when Dorgu scored, a picture of frustration. “I was angry with the situation, not with the players,” he said. A few minutes earlier, the Villa supporters had been jubilant, taunting their former midfielder Youri Tielemans with a chorus of: “Youri, what’s the score?”

Few, Emery included, foresaw the eventual answer. Villa were on course for their biggest victory at Old Trafford since 1920; then, suddenly, they did not have a win at all. This was confusing and complicated, crazy entertainment. United showed a self-destructive streak at the start of each half and reacted to spread the kind of chaos that put a smile back on their faces.

“I am disappointed we didn’t win the game,” claimed Carrick. United were both awful and exciting. They have character, if not competence at the back, where they did an impression of a particularly hungover pub team. A team with a series of historic lows have a pan-European level of porousness. As Villa scored four, no team in Europe’s five major leagues has conceded more goals in all competitions than United. Defensively, they are disastrous, disorganised, struggling at set-pieces, forever caught out by the counter-attack. Dalot is in hideous form and it got worse. Carrick erred by not swapping him with Noussair Mazraoui at half-time. What followed was all too predictable as, unable to contain the outstanding Alysson, Dalot fouled him to concede a penalty. Yet when Dalot eventually did go off, he was replaced by a rescuer, in the shape of the fit-again Dorgu.

Before his introduction, United had looked a shambles as they made a shocking start, and then another. They twice responded to Carrick’s team talks by capitulating, conceding two goals in four minutes at the start of the match and two in eight after the break.

Two goals behind after 18 minutes to Roma, United somehow surpassed that. This was the earliest they had ever been 2-0 down in a Premier League game when Villa doubled their lead, with Senne Lammens at fault for both.

Dalot should share the blame for Alyson’s first-minute opener, allowing the winger too much room to shoot. He beat the goalkeeper at his near post. When Lammens only pushed another Alysson shot straight to Nicolas Jackson, the summer signing slotted in his eighth goal in his last nine games.

It was, ridiculously, the fifth consecutive game in which United went 2-0 down. Briefly, they hinted at a second consecutive 3-2 win, only for something still more outlandish to unfold. The comeback against Roma began with a penalty won by Matheus Cunha and scored by Fernandes. Five days later, Boubacar Kamara fouled the Brazilian and the United captain sent Zion Suzuki the wrong way. Déjà vu.

As United were forced into a pattern of frenetic attacking, Cunha tried to power another fightback. There were echoes of Tuesday night, waves of attack. Cunha, Fernandes and Amad Diallo all came close. Suzuki made fine saves from Cunha and Amad. Tielemans swept in his first United goal from Mazraoui’s cutback.

After the interval, Villa felt fired up again. United emerged dopily. Carrick left Dalot up against the outstanding Alysson and tripped him. Either the winger was unstoppable or United made him look so but John McGinn, who missed his penalty against Fulham last week, scored this.

Then Lammens made his save of the game, sparing Leny Yoro an own goal but in vain. Jackson scuffed his shot but Leon Goretzka finished. His first Villa goal, it seemed, would finish off Carrick and United. Somehow, extraordinarily, it did not. They struck back in added time. His reign may be in added time, too.

#1028. Man Utd are in relegation trouble and Carrick must be sacked

Michael Carrick stood perfectly still and raised his left arm, and his index finger, high in the air. Around him, chaos. As it had been all afternoon. Substitute Patrick Dorgu had just headed in a corner to rescue a point for Manchester United in the 96th minute and, maybe, save Carrick his job.

Going into added time and United were two goals behind. It seemed all was lost for them against Aston Villa and for their head coach, but how telling was the reaction, in the directors’ box, of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, who both jumped up in celebration? They were far more animated than Carrick and could not contain themselves.

"Football is a contact sport!" 🗣️ Did Senne Lammens foul Zion Suzuki for Man United's equaliser? 🤔 https://t.co/KCb1lHqPHP

Did their behaviour betray not just their excitement in the moment but their relief at not having to sack Carrick during this forthcoming international break? If so, they need to think again. They need to make a sober and rational decision based on evidence. And the evidence shows that Carrick must go. Because this kind of football is unsustainable. This kind of football does not work. This kind of football is stupid.

United are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. When they play Liverpool away, their next game, on November 22, it will be the first time they have done so from inside the relegation zone since March 1937.

They appear shockingly disorganised. Tactics seem to be an after-thought; where motivation is lacking until desperation kicks in. United conceded two goals within four minutes at the start of the game. And then two more within eight minutes of the second half kicking off.

The bottom line is this: can they afford not to make a change? If they do not, United could be accused of copping out and gambling with their status. So, Berrada and Wilcox must ask: what is Carrick doing in the dressing room and the training ground? What messages are he and his assistant Steve Holland sending out? Are the players even listening?

At the end the fans sang Carrick’s name after United became the first team in the Premier League to come back twice from being two goals down. That also summed up the fog of confusion at a club who so obviously lack direction – from the top down – and need to get a grip of themselves. Carrick talked about having to “tighten up” the defending. But everything needs to be stronger. More taut. More competitive.

Chaos can be entertaining. Chaos can be fun. As an advert for the Premier League this was outstanding. United fans will be thrilled with the Fergie-time comeback. But chaos is also unsustainable. No one knows what to expect from United.

In the cold light of day Villa manager Unai Emery will have to ask himself whether he, too, got it wrong. His substitutions did not work, bizarrely taking off too much experience, such as his outstanding captain John McGinn, and he handed United a late initiative when it looked like all hope was lost.

But analyse the goals that United conceded. Any rational response would suggest a change should be made. Take the first two. Villa scored with their first attack, moving the ball from a throw-in, with zero pressure on them, from left to right with McGinn finding Alysson. The winger’s low first-time shot went through the legs of goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who had an awful game. Lammens’s only positive contribution was to come up for the late corner from which Dorgu scored, possibly getting away with a sly nudge on Villa’s Zion Suzuki.

What a start for Aston Villa! 🔥 Alysson fires home to give the the visitors the lead https://t.co/F0nfSRMWRa

Then Lammens conceded a second as he fumbled a shot from Alysson, after the Brazilian was again teed up by McGinn with Nicolas Jackson tucking home the rebound. It followed a poor defensive header from Leny Yoro. It would not be his last one.

Nicolas Jackson has made it 2-0 to Aston Villa after just 4 minutes and boos ring out around Old Trafford 🤯 https://t.co/G7oWDNMjGS

At that point, even so early, it felt over. For United. For Carrick. Then it got complicated. In fairness, United responded brilliantly. By half-time it was 2-2 and a potentially mutinous situation, with the fans on edge and unfurling new banners attacking the hierarchy – including one which read “your funeral not ours” – had turned and were raucous in a positive way.

Matheus Cunha, with a sharp turn and run into the Villa penalty area before being brought down, earned the spot kick from which Bruno Fernandes pulled back the first goal. Former Villa midfielder Youri Tielemans drew them level with a first-time shot. Not just that but they peppered the Villa goal.

Youri Tielemans against his former club! 😱 Manchester United are level just before the break! https://t.co/8kFOQkl814

Then they conceded two more in quick succession with a ridiculous trip on Alysson by Diogo Dalot, who was given the runaround at left-back until he was substituted to cheers. McGinn scored from the penalty. It was 4-2 when Yoro inexplicably headed a McGinn free-kick goalwards, Lammens tipped it on to the crossbar and Leon Goretzka eventually bundled the ball in.

Tellingly, the United supporters appeared too stunned to protest. The game meandered to what felt like an inevitable conclusion, petering out much like, surely, Carrick’s time in charge.

But, football, bloody hell. As someone – who was appointed United manager 40 years ago last week – once said. Dorgu made a difference. As did Joshua Zirkzee, another substitute, as the pair became United’s unlikely saviours, the striker sweeping home the full-back’s cross in the 92nd minute, with six added on.

Then a corner was won. The roar went up – as did Lammens. But it was Dorgu who met the delivery from close range to salvage a point. But the big question is: did he also salvage Carrick?

Michael Carrick has insisted he remains the right man to lead Manchester United and will not walk away despite the club being marooned in the relegation zone.

United came from 2-0 and 4-2 down to claim a last gasp 4-4 draw against Aston Villa thanks to Patrick Dorgu’s dramatic 96th-minute equaliser on another wild day at Old Trafford.It means United still only have one Premier League win to their name this season and are languishing in 18th position, a point adrift of safety, heading into the international break when the Old Trafford hierarchy must decide whether to keep faith with Carrick or appoint their third manager this year.

Carrick cut a spiky figure when asked about his future by Sky Sports and whether he would walk away.

“That’s not going to happen,” Carrick said, before asking “will there?” when it was put to him that there would “clearly” be conversations about his future.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on the things we’ve been working on and showing a lot of good in the game today,” he said. “Tighten up on some things and start winning football matches.”

"That's not going to happen" 🗣️ Michael Carrick responds to the notion that he could resign as Manchester United head coach 🔴 https://t.co/q1fBKSXL7l

But we can do something about it.”

Roy Keane, the former United captain, likened Carrick to a “politician”. “It’s hard to believe what’s coming out of the United camp because we can’t even be sure they’re being honest with themselves. Carrick defended Dalot’s contributions after another dismal showing from the Portugal defender and claimed the fans were “right behind” the players, despite growing discontent in the stands.

I understand the situation, we haven’t won enough games, but I expect to carry on working on the things that we’ve been working on, tightening things up and winning football matches.

Disappointed that we didn’t win the game. Thought we were the better team for large parts, keeping making it difficult for ourselves with some of the goals we are giving away. Not just one, it’s two in quick succession.

Came back into the game, had a lot of the game and could have won it. It’s moments that we need to tighten up on. Different moments, individual moments, we are giving away different goals that you wouldn’t normally see.

There was a lot of good in that performance.

Before we played everyone is a fan. You understand why they are frustrated. This is completely fine, we understand. We are on the pitch and we need to manage this. We need to change the mentality – be in the game. I don’t think the fans are against us it’s just that they want to see us perform and win games.

Before anything else we need to look inside to us - the players, the staff. It’s a huge club and to feel something like this [being in relegation zone] is not normal - we need to come back. Many more things to do, we have lots more games. We need to learn from the last seasons. We can not do the same things. We’re good enough to go and change our situation - fight for us, the players and staff. We only ask for the fans to keep doing what they are doing because it helps us.

So disappointed, after the other night we talked a lot about how not to concede goals and then change our mentality to come again. We did it again, conceded goals. We can’t do that – we need to play like Man Utd and go forward and create chances, play with more courage. After we concede goals we show character but if we do this before we can win much more games.

We want to be the best and show that we can come back. We need to show the mentality to do this from the start.
